title: Total communication and assessing communication
blurb: Use every channel a person understands, assess expressive and receptive communication, and check understanding before you act.
question: Delroy, 42, has a moderate learning disability and is admitted to a medical ward. He answers 'yes' to every question the doctor asks, including two that contradict each other. How should the nurse assess and support his communication?

teach.h: Every channel, matched to the person
teach.body: Total communication means using every available means to understand and be understood: speech, signs, symbols, photos, objects, gestures, facial expression, body language, writing and technology, chosen to suit the individual. In plain English: do not rely on words alone. Find out how this person takes in information and how they let others know what they want, then use those channels every time.
teach.cite: Standard learning disability practice; NMC Annexe A 2.5

teach.caption: NICE NG11 defines both and asks assessors to consider each one. One can be much stronger than the other.

teach.h: Information in a form the person can use
teach.body: NICE NG11 asks staff to give information in a format and language suited to the person's cognitive and developmental level, including spoken and picture formats and written versions in Easy Read with different colours and fonts. The Accessible Information Standard requires services to identify, record, flag, share, meet and review a person's information and communication needs, recording the need itself, not just the diagnosis.
teach.cite: NICE NG11 1.1.1; Accessible Information Standard DAPB1605 (2025)

teach.caption: Most people use several channels at once. Combine them rather than picking one.

teach.body: Hearing loss and sight problems are common in people with a learning disability and may be unrecognised (NICE NG96 lists both as conditions to monitor). Visual impairment is a risk factor for self-injury and stereotypy (NICE NG11 1.4.1). Before deciding someone 'cannot understand', check that hearing aids and glasses are in and working, reduce background noise, face the person in good light and allow time to respond.

teach.caption: Teach-back works better than 'Do you understand?', which invites a 'yes'.

teach.h: Scenario: Delroy on a medical ward
teach.body: Delroy says 'yes' to everything, which may be a learned way to please rather than real agreement. The nurse reads his passport, which says he understands short phrases with pictures and uses some signs. She replaces closed questions with simple choices shown on cards, asks him to point, and uses teach-back. She records his communication needs on the record and flags them so every shift uses the same approach, and involves his support worker.

teach.text: Good speech does not prove good understanding, and no speech does not mean no understanding. Judge expressive and receptive skills separately, and do not use a string of 'yes' answers as evidence of consent or comprehension.

items: Total communication: every channel (speech, sign, symbol, object, gesture, technology) matched to the person.
Assess expressive (telling) and receptive (understanding) communication separately.
Ask the person first, then those who know them; read the passport.
Check hearing aids, glasses, light and noise before judging understanding.
AIS: identify, record, flag, share, meet and review the need.

summary: You can now assess a person's expressive and receptive communication, use every channel that works for them, and check understanding with chunk-and-check rather than closed questions. You can record and share communication needs under the Accessible Information Standard.

A.q: A student nurse asks what 'total communication' means in learning disability care. Which description is most accurate?
options: Using every method that suits the person to understand and be understood
Using Makaton signs with every person who has a learning disability
Speaking slowly and loudly so that the person can follow speech
Writing all information down so the person can reread it later
A.why: Total communication combines every available channel (speech, signs, symbols, objects, gestures, technology) chosen to fit the individual.

whyNot.1: Makaton is one tool; total communication is broader and individualised.
whyNot.2: Raising volume does not help understanding and relies on speech alone.
whyNot.3: Written text is one channel and may not suit someone who does not read.

A.q: Grace, 30, has a learning disability and speaks in full sentences. Her carer says she 'understands much less than she says'. Which aspect of communication is the carer describing?
options: Expressive communication that is weaker than her speech
Sensory communication linked to her hearing
Receptive communication that is weaker than her speech
Social communication linked to her eye contact
A.why: Receptive communication is understanding; expressive is getting a message across. Grace's expressive speech is stronger than her receptive understanding.

whyNot.0: Her expressive speech is good; the concern is understanding.
whyNot.1: Nothing suggests a hearing problem; the description is about comprehension.
whyNot.3: Eye contact and social interaction are not what the carer describes.

A.q: Under the Accessible Information Standard, what should a nurse record about a person's communication?
options: The diagnosis of learning disability on the front sheet
The specific support the person needs to communicate
A note that the person lacks capacity to communicate
The name of the family member who speaks for them
A.why: The Standard asks services to record the person's information and communication need (for example 'needs pictures and short phrases'), not just the diagnosis, then flag, share and meet it.

whyNot.0: A diagnosis does not tell staff what support to give.
whyNot.2: Capacity is decision-specific and is not a communication record.
whyNot.3: Family can help, but the record is about how the person communicates.

B.q: Hamid, 55, has a learning disability and does not respond when the nurse explains his blood test. Staff assume he does not understand. Which action should come first?
options: Ask his sister to explain the procedure to him later
Repeat the explanation more slowly and in a louder voice
Record that he lacks capacity to consent to blood tests
Check that his hearing aids are in and working
B.why: Hearing loss is common and may be the barrier. Before judging understanding, check sensory aids, face him in good light and reduce noise.

whyNot.0: Delegating the explanation skips the simple check of whether he can hear.
whyNot.1: Raising the voice does not fix a hearing aid that is missing or not working.
whyNot.2: Capacity cannot be judged before all practicable steps to help him understand are taken.

B.q: A nurse explains discharge medicines to Rosie, who has a mild learning disability. Which approach best checks that Rosie has understood?
options: Ask 'Do you understand what I have told you?'
Ask Rosie to show which tablet she takes at night
Give her the printed leaflet from the medicine box
Ask her mother to sign the discharge checklist
B.why: Teach-back (asking the person to show or say it back) checks real understanding, especially when the information is given in small chunks with pictures.

whyNot.0: A closed question invites 'yes' and does not test understanding.
whyNot.2: A standard leaflet may not be accessible to Rosie.
whyNot.3: A relative's signature does not show that Rosie understands.

B.q: Ellie, 24, has a severe learning disability and limited speech. Which source should the nurse use first to learn how she communicates?
options: Ellie herself and the people who know her well
The learning disability liaison team's standard leaflet
A formal speech and language therapy assessment
The GP referral letter that lists her diagnoses
B.why: Start with the person and those who know them (family, carers, passport). They know her signs, sounds and gestures and how she shows yes and no.

whyNot.1: A generic leaflet does not describe Ellie's own communication.
whyNot.2: SLT may help later, but the first step is to ask her and those who know her.
whyNot.3: A list of diagnoses does not say how she communicates.

C.q: Delroy, 42, has a moderate learning disability. During a ward round he says 'yes' to whether he has pain and 'yes' to whether he is pain-free. What is the nurse's best next step?
options: Record that he has no pain because he said so last
Assess him as lacking capacity because his answers conflict
Offer simple picture choices and ask him to point
Ask the doctor to rephrase both questions more slowly
C.why: Repeated 'yes' answers may be acquiescence. Offering simple visual choices and asking him to point gives a more reliable answer; then confirm with his passport and carers.

whyNot.0: His last answer is not reliable when his answers contradict each other.
whyNot.1: Inconsistent answers to closed questions do not show incapacity; practicable steps come first.
whyNot.3: Slower closed questions still invite 'yes'; the format needs to change.

C.q: Priya, 33, is autistic with a learning disability and uses a picture board. She is transferred to a new ward at night without her board. Next morning she is distressed and hitting the table. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give her the PRN medication prescribed for agitation
Ask her to stop and to use her words to explain
Move her to a side room until she becomes calm
Find her picture board and ask what she needs
C.why: Priya has lost her main expressive channel. Restoring it lets her communicate the need behind her distress; the transfer should have included her communication aid.

whyNot.0: Medication before restoring her means of communication treats the symptom, not the need.
whyNot.1: Asking for words ignores that her board is how she communicates.
whyNot.2: Isolating her does not address the missing communication aid.

C.q: A ward is reviewing how it meets the Accessible Information Standard for people with a learning disability. Which step of the Standard makes sure a person's needs follow them when they move between services?
options: Identifying the need at the first appointment
Recording the person's preferred name and pronouns
Sharing the recorded need with the next service
Meeting the need during the hospital stay
C.why: The Standard requires needs to be shared (with consent where required) with other services, so the next team meets them without re-assessing. Transfers are where communication aids and needs are lost.

whyNot.0: Identifying is the start of the process; the question asks about moving between services.
whyNot.1: Preferred name matters but is not the AIS sharing step.
whyNot.3: Meeting the need on the ward does not help the next service unless the need is shared.

reteach.title: Two directions of traffic
reteach.question: Picture communication as a two-way road. What travels each way, and what can block it?

blocks.body: Information travels in (receptive: what the person understands) and out (expressive: how they tell you). Either lane can be blocked by hearing loss, sight loss, noise, jargon, too much at once, or a missing aid such as a picture board. Total communication opens every lane you can.

explain.body: Use every channel that works for the person: speech, signs, symbols, photos, objects, gestures and technology, often together.

test.q: Which plan best reflects a total communication approach for a person with a moderate learning disability?
options: Speak clearly and use written instructions
Use the communication method staff know best
Wait for a speech and language therapist first
Combine speech, signs and pictures they recognise
test.why: Total communication combines the channels the person uses and recognises.

whyNot.0: Speech and writing alone may not reach the person.
whyNot.1: The method must suit the person, not the staff.
whyNot.2: Communication cannot wait; use what is known now and refer if needed.

explain.body: Expressive: how the person gets a message across. Receptive: how much they understand. They can differ, so assess both.

test.q: A man with a learning disability uses no speech but follows two-step spoken instructions. How should his communication be described?
options: Limited expressive, stronger receptive skills
Limited receptive, stronger expressive skills
Both expressive and receptive skills absent
Both expressive and receptive skills typical
test.why: He understands spoken instructions (receptive) but does not use speech to express himself (expressive).

whyNot.3: Having no speech shows an expressive difficulty.

explain.body: Hearing and sight problems are common and often missed. Check aids, light and noise before deciding someone cannot understand.

test.q: A woman with Down syndrome seems not to follow verbal instructions on the ward. What should the nurse check first?
options: Whether her family can attend to translate
Whether she can hear and see clearly
Whether she has capacity to make decisions
Whether a sedative is needed for procedures
test.why: Hearing and vision problems are common in Down syndrome and can be mistaken for lack of understanding.

whyNot.0: Family help is useful but does not address a sensory barrier.
whyNot.2: Capacity is assessed only after practicable steps such as sensory checks.
whyNot.3: Sedation does not address a communication barrier.

explain.body: The Accessible Information Standard: identify, record, flag, share, meet and review communication needs. Record the need, not just the diagnosis.

test.q: Which record best meets the Accessible Information Standard for a man with a learning disability?
options: Has a learning disability and is non-verbal
Lacks capacity; speak to his father
Uses Makaton signs; needs pictures for choices
Communication difficulties noted at admission
test.why: The Standard asks for the specific need so staff know exactly what support to give.

whyNot.0: A diagnosis and 'non-verbal' do not tell staff what to do.
whyNot.1: Capacity is decision-specific and this does not record his communication need.
whyNot.3: A vague note does not say how to meet the need.
